templates.scenario: A computer at {workplace|the} will not connect to the network.
templates.prompt: Put these troubleshooting steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Check the simple things first, such as power and cable connections
Restart the device and try again
Write down any error message and look up the steps in the help guide
Contact IT support and describe what you already tried

precedence.why: Simple causes are quick to check and rule out before anything else.
A restart clears many problems, so try it before digging into error messages.
IT support can help faster when you can tell them the error and what you tried.

templates.principle: Troubleshoot from simplest to most involved, and give IT support clear details when you ask for help.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {System|the} will not load on your computer while {client|a} is waiting. The connection icon looks normal, and you have not restarted the program.

options.text: Close and reopen the program, check your connection, and report the problem to IT if it still will not load.
options.why: Quick checks solve many problems in a minute, and reporting afterward gives IT useful detail. It also keeps the wait short for the person.

options.text: Uninstall and reinstall the whole program right away to make sure the problem is gone for good.
options.why: Reinstalling is a big step that may remove settings or need permissions you do not have. Simple checks come first.
options.misconception: The biggest fix is always the most reliable.

options.text: Tell {client|a} the system is down for the day without trying anything else.
options.why: Announcing an outage before checking can mislead the person and may be wrong if a restart would fix it.
options.misconception: If it does not load, it is broken.

options.text: Ask a coworker to do your task on their computer without mentioning the problem to anyone.
options.why: Passing the task along may help for now, but the problem stays hidden, and you could be asking someone to stop what they are doing.
options.misconception: Working around a problem is the same as solving it.

templates.principle: Start troubleshooting with quick, low-risk checks, then report to IT with what you tried.
templates.timing: Quick checks come first and reporting second.

templates.scenario: {Workplace|the} uses an approved shared drive for work files. You need to send a large {document|a} to {coworker} for review today. You have used a personal email account and a free public file-sharing site for other things.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Save the file to the approved shared drive, and share a link with {coworker} through it.
options.why: The approved drive is set up for work files, with access controls and backups. Using it keeps the file where the workplace can manage it.

options.text: Send it from your personal email account, since it gets to {coworker} the fastest.
options.why: Personal accounts are outside what the workplace manages, so the file could be hard to protect or recover later.
options.misconception: The fastest method is the best method.

options.text: Upload it to the free public site you already know, then send {coworker} the link.
options.why: A public site may not protect the file and is not set up by your workplace. Convenience does not make it approved.
options.misconception: A tool I already use is fine for work.

options.text: Copy it onto a personal USB drive and give it to {coworker} in person.
options.why: A loose drive can be lost or carry problems, and the file ends up outside the approved place for work files.
options.misconception: Hand-delivery is always safer than online.

templates.principle: Use the file-sharing tools your workplace has approved for work files, rather than personal accounts or public sites.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. Your {lead} asks you to keep track of weekly hours for twenty people and show each person's total. The numbers change every week, and totals need to update when a number is changed.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate tool?

options.text: Use a spreadsheet with formulas, so totals update automatically when a number changes.
options.why: A spreadsheet is built for numbers that change and for totals that must stay correct, so each update takes one edit.

options.text: Type the hours into a word-processing document, and add them up with a calculator each week.
options.why: A word-processing document stores text well but does not calculate, so every change means re-adding by hand, which invites mistakes.
options.misconception: Any program that holds numbers will do.

options.text: Make one presentation slide per person, and update each slide by hand when hours change.
options.why: Slides are meant for presenting, not for tracking. Twenty slides would be slow to update and hard to total.
options.misconception: A visual format is always clearer.

options.text: Keep the hours in a text message thread, and total them up at the end of each week.
options.why: Message threads are hard to search and to correct, and totals would have to be worked out by hand every time.
options.misconception: The simplest tool is always the best tool.

templates.principle: Choose software that fits the task: spreadsheets for changing numbers and totals, documents for text, slides for presenting.

templates.scenario: {Workplace|the} has approved a writing assistant tool for drafting general messages. Its policy says employees must not enter {client|a}'s personal details into it, and must review every draft before sending. You need to write a reply to {client|a} about an account problem.

options.text: Ask the tool for general wording without any personal details, then review it and add the specifics yourself.
options.why: This uses the approved tool within its limits and keeps your own review as the final step, which the policy requires.

options.text: Skip the tool and write the whole reply yourself, since the policy limits what you can enter.
options.why: This is safe and follows the policy, but it does not use the approved tool for the part it is allowed to help with.
options.misconception: If a tool has limits, it is easiest not to use it.

options.text: Paste the message and the account details into the tool for a faster draft, then check it before sending.
options.why: Reviewing the draft is required, but entering personal details breaks the policy, and checking afterward does not undo the disclosure.
options.misconception: A careful review afterward makes up for sharing details.

options.text: Let the tool write the whole reply from a general description and send it as written to save time.
options.why: The policy requires a review of every draft. Unreviewed text can contain mistakes or the wrong tone.
options.misconception: If a tool is approved, its output is ready to send.

templates.principle: Use approved tools within their stated limits, keep protected details out of them, and review what they produce before it goes out.

templates.scenario: A coworker at {workplace|the} writes this note about a computer update.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is a problem.

segments.text: Plan for this week's computer maintenance:
I will save my open files before the update starts.
segments.whyFine: Saving work before an update is a sensible precaution.

segments.text: I will keep postponing the restart for a month, because updates are annoying and probably unnecessary.
segments.why: Updates often include fixes for problems and security risks, so putting them off for a month leaves the device exposed.

segments.text: I will tell IT if the update takes longer than expected.
segments.whyFine: Reporting a problem to IT is appropriate.

templates.principle: Install updates promptly; postponing them leaves known problems unfixed.

templates.scenario: An inventory spreadsheet has item names, quantities, and reorder dates. Your lead wants the earliest reorder date first without mixing up the item records.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Sort complete records by reorder date.
options.why: Sorting whole records preserves the relationship between each item and its date.

options.text: Sort only the date column.
options.why: Dates would no longer reliably match the corresponding items.
options.misconception: Dates would no longer reliably match the corresponding items.

options.text: Filter out items with later dates.
options.why: Filtering hides records rather than ordering all of them.
options.misconception: Filtering hides records rather than ordering all of them.

options.text: Change the date format in every cell.
options.why: Formatting changes appearance, not row order.
options.misconception: Formatting changes appearance, not row order.

templates.principle: Sort the full range when the columns in each row belong together.

templates.scenario: A sales worksheet lists quantities in column B and unit prices in column C. Row 2 needs a total that updates if its quantity changes.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Multiply B2 by C2 with a formula.
options.why: The formula uses the quantity and unit price from the same row.

options.text: Type the total from a calculator into the cell.
options.why: A fixed number does not update when its inputs change.
options.misconception: A fixed number does not update when its inputs change.

options.text: Add the quantity and price with a formula.
options.why: Adding quantity and price does not calculate extended cost.
options.misconception: Adding quantity and price does not calculate extended cost.

options.text: Multiply the quantity and price from row 3 instead.
options.why: Those references point to another record.
options.misconception: Those references point to another record.

templates.principle: Use cell references and the appropriate operation when a spreadsheet result needs to update.

review.notes: Original scenario. The necessary conditions are given in the prompt.

templates.scenario: A shared order table contains open and closed orders. A coworker needs to see only open orders without deleting any rows or changing another user’s view. The spreadsheet supports private filter views.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Create a private filter view for the Open status.
options.why: The view limits the displayed rows while preserving the shared data and other views.

options.text: Delete the closed rows and recover them later.
options.why: Deleting rows changes the underlying shared data.
options.misconception: Deleting rows changes the underlying shared data.

options.text: Sort by status and leave all rows visible.
options.why: Sorting groups rows but does not meet the request to show only open ones.
options.misconception: Sorting groups rows but does not meet the request to show only open ones.

options.text: Create a shared filter that changes the whole team’s view.
options.why: The request calls for a private view.
options.misconception: The request calls for a private view.

templates.principle: Use a filter view to see a subset of shared data without deleting records.

review.notes: Original scenario. The necessary conditions are given in the prompt.

templates.scenario: A long training document needs navigable section headings. Its editor offers built-in heading styles.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Apply heading styles to section titles in the correct hierarchy.
options.why: Heading styles convey document structure to navigation tools and assistive technology.

options.text: Make each title bold and larger without using styles.
options.why: Visual emphasis alone does not add heading structure.
options.misconception: Visual emphasis alone does not add heading structure.

options.text: Put each title inside a screenshot.
options.why: The words become harder to navigate or edit.
options.misconception: The words become harder to navigate or edit.

options.text: Insert extra blank lines above each title.
options.why: Spacing alone does not create navigable headings.
options.misconception: Spacing alone does not create navigable headings.

templates.principle: Use semantic headings to make a document easier to navigate.

review.notes: Original scenario. The necessary conditions are given in the prompt.

templates.scenario: A supervisor wants to review your revisions to an existing manual before accepting them. The word processor can track edits.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Turn on change tracking and revise the manual in the shared review copy.
options.why: Tracked changes let the reviewer see and accept or reject individual edits.

options.text: Replace the manual with a clean copy and discard the old one.
options.why: The reviewer loses the revision history.
options.misconception: The reviewer loses the revision history.

options.text: Highlight every revised paragraph without recording deletions.
options.why: Highlighting does not show what was removed.
options.misconception: Highlighting does not show what was removed.

options.text: Send a screenshot of the new pages.
options.why: A screenshot cannot be used to accept or reject edits.
options.misconception: A screenshot cannot be used to accept or reject edits.

templates.principle: Use revision tracking when a reviewer needs to approve specific changes.

review.notes: Original scenario. The necessary conditions are given in the prompt.

templates.scenario: A handbook repeats an old building name. It also quotes an archived notice where that name must remain. The editor has Find and Replace.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Review each match and replace only current references.
options.why: Checking the context preserves the required archived quotation.

options.text: Replace all matches at once.
options.why: That also changes the archived quotation.
options.misconception: That also changes the archived quotation.

options.text: Search for the new name and delete its matches.
options.why: That does not identify old references.
options.misconception: That does not identify old references.

options.text: Change only the first match and assume the rest are duplicates.
options.why: Other current references may still need updating.
options.misconception: Other current references may still need updating.

templates.principle: Use reviewable replacements when identical text has different purposes.

review.notes: Original scenario. The necessary conditions are given in the prompt.

templates.scenario: A project folder contains two draft files and one file marked Approved. Your lead asks for the version authorized for distribution.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Verify the revision of the approved distribution copy.
options.why: Approval and revision identify the intended distribution copy.

options.text: Send the file with the largest size.
options.why: File size does not establish approval.
options.misconception: File size does not establish approval.

options.text: Send all copies so recipients can pick.
options.why: That risks distributing drafts and shifting the decision to recipients.
options.misconception: That risks distributing drafts and shifting the decision to recipients.

options.text: Rename the newest draft Approved and send it.
options.why: Renaming cannot grant approval.
options.misconception: Renaming cannot grant approval.

templates.principle: Use the documented approval and revision when choosing a file to distribute.

review.notes: Original scenario. The necessary conditions are given in the prompt.

templates.scenario: A workstation has enough memory to open its apps but reports almost no free space when saving a large video. The media team has an approved storage location with room.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Save the project to the approved location with sufficient storage.
options.why: The error is about persistent storage space for the file.

options.text: Close the monitor settings window and retry.
options.why: That does not create space to save the file.
options.misconception: That does not create space to save the file.

options.text: Increase the screen resolution to fit the video.
options.why: Screen resolution does not add storage capacity.
options.misconception: Screen resolution does not add storage capacity.

options.text: Connect a larger external keyboard to the workstation.
options.why: An input device does not affect available storage.
options.misconception: An input device does not affect available storage.

templates.principle: Distinguish file storage from working memory and input or display hardware.

review.notes: Original scenario. The necessary conditions are given in the prompt.

templates.scenario: An approved site is slow in one browser profile. The same site opens normally on the same computer in a clean profile.
templates.prompt: Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Report a profile-specific problem and note recent profile changes.
options.why: The comparison narrows the issue to a difference between profiles.

options.text: Report that the entire company network is down.
options.why: The site works in another profile on the same computer.
options.misconception: The site works in another profile on the same computer.

options.text: Replace the monitor to speed up the page.
options.why: The profile test does not implicate the display.
options.misconception: The profile test does not implicate the display.

options.text: Delete shared files to free space without asking.
options.why: That risks data loss and does not follow the evidence.
options.misconception: That risks data loss and does not follow the evidence.

templates.principle: Change one variable when troubleshooting and report what the comparison isolates.
